2.3.1.examLens: Keep accuracy and precision straight, know the five components of measurement error, and use the variance relationship to back out true process variation.

worked.question: A process shows an observed standard deviation of 0.50 mm. A gage study shows the measurement system's standard deviation is 0.30 mm. (a) What is the true process standard deviation? (b) Repeated readings of a master are 10.21, 10.20, 10.22, and 10.21 against a true value of 10.00. Accurate, precise, both, or neither?
worked.solution:
(a) σ(process) = √(0.50² − 0.30²) = √(0.25 − 0.09) = √0.16 = 0.40 mm.
(b) The readings cluster tightly (precise) but sit about 0.21 above the true value (not accurate). Precise but not accurate.

2.3.2.examLens: Read a description and name the type of location error.

worked.question: Name the error: (a) a micrometer reads 0.02 mm high on 5 mm, 0.05 mm high on 25 mm, and 0.09 mm high on 50 mm parts; (b) a scale that was correct in January reads 2 grams high by June; (c) a caliper reads exactly 0.03 mm high on every part.

2.3.3.examLens: This is a calculation topic with an interpretation step. Compute the metrics, then decide whether the gage is acceptable and what to fix.

worked.question: A study gives repeatability SD = 0.020, reproducibility SD = 0.030, and part-to-part SD = 0.200. The tolerance (USL − LSL) is 1.0. Compute GRR, total variation, %SV, %Tolerance, %Contribution, and ndc, then decide.
worked.solution:
GRR = √(0.020² + 0.030²) = √(0.0004 + 0.0009) = √0.0013 = 0.0361.
Total variation = √(0.0013 + 0.2²) = √0.0413 = 0.2032.
%SV = 0.0361 ÷ 0.2032 = 17.7%.
%Tolerance = 6 × 0.0361 ÷ 1.0 = 21.6%.
%Contribution = 0.0013 ÷ 0.0413 = 3.1%.
ndc = 1.41 × (0.200 ÷ 0.0361) = 1.41 × 5.54 = 7.8, truncated to 7.
Decision: %SV and %Tolerance both fall in the 10 to 30% band, so the gage is conditionally acceptable depending on the application. ndc is 7, which meets the 5 or more requirement. Reproducibility (0.030) is larger than repeatability (0.020), so operator technique or training is the first place to look.

2.3.4.examLens: Know which MSA fits which data, and interpret kappa and misclassification results. The classic trap is that appraisers can agree and still be wrong.

worked.question: An inspector makes 100 decisions against a known standard: 40 opportunities were good parts and 60 were bad parts. The inspector called 4 good parts bad and 3 bad parts good. Compute effectiveness, miss rate, and false-alarm rate. Separately, if Po = 0.88 and Pe = 0.52, what is kappa?
worked.solution:
Errors = 4 + 3 = 7. Effectiveness = 93 ÷ 100 = 93%.
Miss rate = 3 ÷ 60 = 5%. False-alarm rate = 4 ÷ 40 = 10%.
Kappa = (0.88 − 0.52) ÷ (1 − 0.52) = 0.36 ÷ 0.48 = 0.75, which just meets the AIAG "good" guideline.

2.3.1.a.title: Accuracy versus precision
2.3.1.a.html:
• Accuracy: how close measurements are to the true (reference) value.
  • Precision: how close repeated measurements are to each other (the spread).

Picture darts on a board. A tight cluster in the wrong spot is precise but not accurate. A wide scatter centered on the bullseye is accurate on average but not precise.

2.3.1.b.title: Resolution (discrimination)
2.3.1.b.html:
Resolution is the smallest increment the gage can show. A common rule is that the increments should be about one-tenth or finer of the tolerance or the process spread.
Example: a tolerance of 0.5 mm calls for a gage that reads to 0.05 mm or finer. A gage that reads only to the nearest 0.5 mm cannot tell parts apart.

2.3.1.c.title: Observed variation includes measurement variation
2.3.1.c.html:
σ²(observed) = σ²(process) + σ²(measurement). Variances add, standard deviations do not.
Example: the observed standard deviation is 5 and the measurement system's is 3. True process σ = √(25 − 9) = √16 = 4.

2.3.1.e.title: Calibration
2.3.1.e.html: Calibration compares the gage against a reference standard (traceable to a recognized authority) and adjusts it. It addresses bias. It does not repair a gage that is imprecise.

2.3.1.f.title: The target analogy
2.3.1.f.html: A tight cluster far from the center is precise but not accurate. Questions describe a picture or numbers and ask which word applies.

2.3.2.a.title: Bias
2.3.2.a.html:
Bias = average of the measurements − the reference value.
Example: a master part is 10.00. The gage averages 10.05. Bias = +0.05.

2.3.2.b.title: Linearity
2.3.2.b.html: How the bias changes across the operating range of the gage. A gage might be right on small parts and read progressively higher on larger ones.

2.3.2.c.title: Stability
2.3.2.c.html: How the bias changes over time (drift). It is monitored by measuring a master part at regular intervals and plotting the results on a control chart.

2.3.2.d.title: Corrective action
2.3.2.d.html:
The fix depends on the pattern.

  • Bias: calibration or adjustment.
  • Linearity: a different gage or method (a single adjustment will not fix an error that changes with size).
  • Stability: look at environment, wear, maintenance, or time effects.

2.3.2.e.title: Name the error
2.3.2.e.html:
• "Reads higher on larger parts" = linearity.
  • "Drifts over several weeks" = stability.
  • "Consistently reads high by the same amount" = bias.

2.3.3.a.title: Repeatability
2.3.3.a.html: Variation when the same operator measures the same part with the same gage several times. Also called equipment variation.

2.3.3.b.title: Reproducibility
2.3.3.b.html: Variation between operators measuring the same parts. Also called appraiser variation.

2.3.3.f.title: % Tolerance
2.3.3.f.html: %Tolerance = 6 × GRR ÷ (USL − LSL) × 100. Current guidance uses 6σ for the study spread. Older material used 5.15σ. Check which one a question uses.

2.3.3.g.title: % Contribution
2.3.3.g.html: %Contribution uses variances rather than standard deviations: GRR variance ÷ total variance × 100.

2.3.3.h.title: Acceptance guidelines
2.3.3.h.html:
AIAG (as cited by Minitab):

  • Under 10%: acceptable.
  • 10% to 30%: may be acceptable, depending on the application, the cost of the gage, and the cost of repair.
  • Over 30%: unacceptable; improve the measurement system.

Do not call the 10 to 30% band simply "marginal." It is a conditional decision.

2.3.3.i.title: Number of distinct categories (ndc)
2.3.3.i.html: ndc = 1.41 × (part SD ÷ GRR SD). You need ndc of 5 or more. Software truncates ndc to a whole number. Do not round up: 4.9 becomes 4, which fails.

2.3.3.j.title: Typical study design
2.3.3.j.html: About 10 parts that span the process range, 3 operators, 2 to 3 repeat measurements, in random order, with operators blinded to part identity. This is typical, not a required formula.

2.3.3.k.title: Crossed versus nested; ANOVA versus Xbar-R
2.3.3.k.html:
• Crossed: every operator measures every part (non-destructive testing).
  • Nested: each part is measured by only one operator, used when testing destroys the part.
  • The ANOVA method can detect an operator-by-part interaction. The Xbar-R method cannot.

2.3.3.l.title: Reading the graphs
2.3.3.l.html:
• R chart by operator: shows consistency. It should be in control.
  • Xbar chart by operator: the limits reflect gage noise, and the points are part averages. Many points should fall outside the limits, because that means the gage can tell the parts apart.
  • Operator-by-part interaction: lines that cross or diverge mean operators disagree on certain parts.

2.3.3.m.title: Compute %GRR and decide
2.3.3.m.html: Compute the components, then apply the guidelines to %SV and %Tolerance, check ndc, and state the conclusion.

2.3.3.n.title: %Study Var versus %Contribution
2.3.3.n.html: Because variance is the square of the standard deviation, 10% and 30% on %SV correspond to about 1% and 9% on %Contribution.

2.3.3.o.title: Diagnose the pattern
2.3.3.o.html:
• Large repeatability: the equipment, fixture, or method is the issue.
  • Large reproducibility: operator technique, training, or lack of standardization.
  • Significant operator-by-part interaction: operators behave inconsistently on certain parts.

This tells you what to fix. Buying a better gage does not help a reproducibility problem.

2.3.3.p.title: %SV looks marginal but %Tolerance is high
2.3.3.p.html:
For sorting parts or conformance decisions, %Tolerance matters more because it compares measurement error to the spec. For evaluating process improvement, %SV is the better estimate of measurement precision.
Example: %SV = 18% and %Tolerance = 34%. For part sorting, the gage is unacceptable, even though 18% alone looks acceptable.

2.3.4.b.title: Attribute agreement analysis
2.3.4.b.html:
For pass/fail or category judgments. It examines four things:

  • Within appraiser: does each appraiser agree with themselves across trials?
  • Each appraiser versus the standard: does each agree with the known correct answer?
  • Between appraisers: do appraisers agree with each other?
  • All appraisers versus the standard.

2.3.4.c.title: Kappa
2.3.4.c.html:
Kappa = (Po − Pe) ÷ (1 − Pe), where Po is the observed proportion of agreement and Pe is the proportion expected by chance. Kappa of 1 is perfect agreement. Kappa of 0 is agreement no better than chance.
Example: Po = 0.90, Pe = 0.50. Kappa = 0.40 ÷ 0.50 = 0.80.

2.3.4.d.title: Interpreting kappa
2.3.4.d.html:
• AIAG (as cited by Minitab): kappa of 0.75 or more indicates good agreement.
  • Some software uses 0.9 or more = very good, 0.7 to 0.9 = marginal, under 0.7 = unacceptable.
  • Other texts call under 0.40 poor.

Know which source a question points to. It is unclear which convention IASSC prefers, so use the one stated in the question.

2.3.4.e.title: Typical study design
2.3.4.e.html: About 30 to 50 items, a mix of good and bad, 2 to 3 appraisers, 2 to 3 trials.

2.3.4.f.title: Misclassification metrics
2.3.4.f.html:
• Effectiveness = correct decisions ÷ total decisions.
  • Miss rate = bad items called good ÷ opportunities with a bad item.
  • False-alarm rate = good items called bad ÷ opportunities with a good item.

2.3.4.g.title: Interpret a kappa table
2.3.4.g.html: Read the kappa values, apply the guideline stated in the question, and decide whether the inspection process is acceptable.

2.3.4.h.title: Agreement is not accuracy
2.3.4.h.html: Appraisers can agree with themselves and with each other and still all be wrong. Always compare against the known standard.

2.3.4.i.title: Fleiss' versus Cohen's kappa, and Kendall's coefficient
2.3.4.i.html: Recognition only. Cohen's kappa is for two raters. Fleiss' kappa extends it to more than two. Kendall's coefficient is used for ordinal ratings.

2.3.1-1.stem: The observed standard deviation of a process is 10, and the measurement system's standard deviation is 6. What is the true process standard deviation?

2.3.1-2.stem: Repeated readings of a 50.00 mm master are 50.42, 50.41, 50.43, and 50.42. Which statement is correct?
2.3.1-2.explanation: The readings cluster tightly (precise) but sit about 0.42 above the true value (not accurate).

2.3.1-3.stem: A part has a tolerance of 0.8 mm. About how fine should the gage resolution be?

options.html: 0.008 mm or finer is required and anything coarser fails

2.3.1-3.explanation: The rule of thumb is a resolution of about one-tenth of the tolerance or finer. (D is too strict to be a rule.)

2.3.1-4.stem: Which TWO are location (accuracy) errors of a measurement system?
2.3.1-4.explanation: Bias, linearity, and stability are location errors. Repeatability and reproducibility are spread (precision) errors.

2.3.2-1.stem: A master part is certified at 25.00 mm. A gage measures it repeatedly with an average of 25.06 mm. What is the bias?
2.3.2-1.explanation: Bias = average measured value − reference value = 25.06 − 25.00 = +0.06 mm.

2.3.2-2.stem: A gage reads correctly on 5 mm parts but progressively higher on 25 mm and 50 mm parts. Which error is this?
2.3.2-2.explanation: Linearity is bias that changes across the gage's range.

2.3.2-3.stem: A scale that was correct in January reads 2 grams high by June. Which error is this?
2.3.2-3.explanation: Stability is bias that changes over time (drift).

2.3.3-1.stem: A study finds repeatability SD = 0.04, reproducibility SD = 0.03, and part-to-part SD = 0.30. What is %Study Variation?

2.3.3-2.stem: Using GRR = 0.05 and a tolerance width (USL − LSL) of 2.0, what is %Tolerance?

2.3.3-3.stem: Part-to-part SD = 0.30 and GRR SD = 0.05. What is the number of distinct categories?
2.3.3-3.explanation: ndc = 1.41 × (0.30 ÷ 0.05) = 1.41 × 6 = 8.46. Software truncates to 8, which meets the requirement of 5 or more.

2.3.3-4.stem: A gage has %Study Variation of 22%. Using the AIAG guideline, how should it be described?

options.html: Possibly acceptable, depending on the application, gage cost, and repair cost

2.3.3-4.explanation: The 10% to 30% band is a conditional decision, not a simple "marginal."

2.3.3-5.stem: A Gage R&R shows small repeatability but large reproducibility. What is the most likely corrective action?

options.html: Standardize the measurement method and train the operators

2.3.3-5.explanation: Large reproducibility points to differences between operators (technique, training, standardization), not equipment.

2.3.3-6.stem: A study gives ndc = 4.9. Because this rounds to 5, the gage passes the requirement.
2.3.3-6.explanation: Software truncates ndc to a whole number, so 4.9 becomes 4, which fails the requirement of 5 or more.

2.3.3-7.stem: A gage will be used to sort parts against a tight specification. Its %Study Variation is 18%, but its %Tolerance is 34%. What is the best conclusion?

options.html: Unacceptable for sorting, because %Tolerance compares measurement error with the spec width
Acceptable, because the two numbers average below 30%

2.3.3-7.explanation: For conformance decisions, %Tolerance matters most. Over 30% is unacceptable for sorting parts.

2.3.4-1.stem: In an attribute agreement study, the observed agreement is 0.85 and the agreement expected by chance is 0.55. What is kappa?

2.3.4-2.stem: Inspectors classify each part as pass or fail. Which study is appropriate?
2.3.4-2.explanation: Categorical judgments use attribute agreement analysis. Gage R&R is for continuous measurements.

2.3.4-3.stem: Three appraisers agree with themselves and with each other on almost every part, but they often disagree with the known master ratings. What is the best conclusion?

options.html: The inspection is acceptable because the appraisers agree
The appraisers are consistent but not accurate, so the inspection needs correction

2.3.4-3.explanation: Agreement among appraisers is not accuracy. Always check against the known standard.

2.3.4-4.stem: In a study there were 50 opportunities where the part was truly good. An appraiser called 5 of them bad. What is the false-alarm rate?
2.3.4-4.explanation: False-alarm rate = good parts called bad ÷ opportunities with a good part = 5 ÷ 50 = 10%.

2.3.3-1.text: A Gage R&R study gives repeatability SD = 0.1, reproducibility SD = 0.06, and part-to-part SD = 0.2. The tolerance width is 1.0. Compute GRR, total variation, %Study Variation, %Contribution, %Tolerance, and ndc, and give the AIAG verdict on %SV.
2.3.3-1.answer: GRR = √(0.1² + 0.06²) = 0.1166. Total variation = √(0.1166² + 0.2²) = 0.2315. %SV = 50.4%. %Contribution = 25.37%. %Tolerance = 6 × 0.1166 ÷ 1.0 = 70.0%. ndc = 1.41 × 0.2 ÷ 0.1166 = 2.42, truncated to 2. By %SV the gage is unacceptable. The ndc of 2 is below 5, which fails that requirement.

2.3.3-2.answer: GRR = √(0.02² + 0.06²) = 0.0632. Total variation = √(0.0632² + 0.8²) = 0.8025. %SV = 7.9%. %Contribution = 0.62%. %Tolerance = 6 × 0.0632 ÷ 1.0 = 37.9%. ndc = 1.41 × 0.8 ÷ 0.0632 = 17.84, truncated to 17. By %SV the gage is acceptable. However, %Tolerance is 37.9%, over 30%, so it would be unacceptable for sorting parts against the specification.

2.3.3-3.text: A Gage R&R study gives repeatability SD = 0.1, reproducibility SD = 0.06, and part-to-part SD = 0.5. The tolerance width is 1.0. Compute GRR, total variation, %Study Variation, %Contribution, %Tolerance, and ndc, and give the AIAG verdict on %SV.

2.3.4-6.text: In an attribute agreement study the observed agreement is 0.8 and the agreement expected by chance is 0.45. What is kappa, and how does it compare with the AIAG guideline?
2.3.4-6.answer: Kappa = (0.8 − 0.45) ÷ (1 − 0.45) = 0.636. This is below the AIAG 'good' level of 0.75.
